tasks.title: Bridge or ford?
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 1` in `route_in.py`, make a variable called `route`: the text `bridge` when `river_level` is above `ford_limit`, and the text `ford` otherwise. Print it to see it.

Check runs your file with other rivers and limits, including a river exactly at the limit, and reads `route` after the lines under `# Task 1`.
nextSteps: Read tonight's callout near the top of the file.
Write an `if` that asks whether the river is above the limit, ending with a colon.
Give `route` its word on a line moved in under the `if`, and the other word under an `else`.
Print `route`, then change `river_level` at the top and run the file again.
hints: Two answers, one question: is the river above the limit? The lesson's heating example has the same shape.
"Above" leaves out the equal case. The lines under `if` and `else` are moved in by the same few spaces, and both lines with a keyword end with a colon.
The shape is `if river_level ... ford_limit:`, a line under it that gives `route` one word, then `else:` and a line under it that gives the other.

tasks.title: How bad is the wind?
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 2`, make a variable called `wind_warning` from `wind_speed`:

- `stay low` when the wind is 50 or more
- `take care` when it is 30 or more
- `clear` otherwise

Print it to see it. Check tries gales, calm nights, and winds of exactly 50 and exactly 30.
nextSteps: Read the part of the lesson on `elif`.
Decide which question to ask first: Python stops at the first branch that is True.
Write the `if`, the `elif` and the `else`, each giving `wind_warning` its words.
Print it, then try a wind of 60 and a wind of 10 at the top.
hints: Three answers need three branches: `if`, `elif` and `else`, in that order, each lined up under the other.
A gale of 60 is also 30 or more. Since only the first True branch runs, the strictest question has to come first. "Or more" includes the equal case.
The shape is `if wind_speed >= ...:` with the words for the strongest wind, then `elif wind_speed >= ...:`, then `else:`.

tasks.title: Helicopter or stretcher?
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 3`, print one line:

```
Call the helicopter
```

when it is daylight (`daylight` is `True`) and `wind_speed` is below 40, and this line otherwise:

```
Carry the stretcher
```

Check tries daylight and darkness, light winds and gales, and a wind of exactly 40, and looks for exactly one of the two lines among the lines Task 3 prints.
nextSteps: List the two things the helicopter needs.
Pick the word that is True only when both sides are.
Write one `if` that asks both questions, and an `else` for every other case.
Run the file, then set `daylight` to `False` at the top and run it again.
hints: One question with two parts: is it light, and is the wind low enough? If either answer is no, the team carries.
`and` is True only when both sides are. `daylight` is already True or False, so it can stand on its own as one side.
The shape is `if daylight and wind_speed ... 40:`, a `print` of the helicopter line under it, then `else:` and a `print` of the stretcher line.

tasks.title: Is there a name?
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 4`, `casualty_name` holds the casualty's name, or empty text (`""`) when the radio did not catch it, or `None` when nobody has asked yet. When it holds a name, print `Casualty:` and the name, like this:

```
Casualty: Morven Gow
```

Otherwise print this line:

```
Casualty: name not known
```

Check tries two names, empty text and `None`.
nextSteps: Read the part of the lesson on what counts as true.
Ask yourself which of the three kinds of value count as false.
Write one `if` that is True only when there is a name, and an `else`.
Run the file with a name, with `""` and with `None` at the top.
hints: Empty text and `None` both mean "no name", and both count as false in an `if`.

An `if` does not need a comparison: it can ask about a variable on its own, and then it asks whether the value counts as true. Text is never the same as `True`, so comparing it with `True` is always False.
The shape is `if casualty_name:` with a `print` of `Casualty:` and the name under it, then `else:` with a `print` of the not known line.
